flow.diagram_label: Secrets Manager SaaS reference architecture with Edges
flow.s1_desc: Secrets Manager SaaS is a service on the Idira Shared Services platform, next to Identity and Privilege Cloud. Inside your network you run Edges, close to the workloads.
flow.s2_desc: Administrators reach the SaaS console with the platform shared services: user management, SSO and MFA, with audit kept centrally.
flow.s3_desc: Add the Conjur Sync user to a Safe and each account becomes secrets in Secrets Manager, one per property, plus a group with read and execute. When CPM rotates the password, the new value syncs in near real time.
flow.s4_desc: With PAM Self-Hosted, the Vault Synchronizer syncs the Safes that have the ConjurSync LOB user as a member. It authenticates with an API key and encrypts data in transit with an x509 client certificate (mTLS).
flow.s5_desc: Each Edge opens an outbound 443 connection to the tenant, optionally through an explicit HTTP/HTTPS proxy, and replicates secrets and workloads. Nothing on the internet needs to reach the Edge.
flow.s6_desc: The firewall rules also allow outbound 443 to an AWS IoT endpoint in the same region. New and updated secrets and workloads reach the Edges almost immediately; other resources, such as groups, within a few minutes.
flow.s7_desc: A workload calls the load balancer, which picks a healthy Edge. The Edge authenticates it locally (API key, JWT, GCP, client certificate or Azure) and returns the secret with low latency.
flow.s8_desc: Authentication and secret retrieval stay on the Edge. Dynamic secret requests, certificate requests and every other action are forwarded to Secrets Manager SaaS.
flow.s9_desc: If the link to the SaaS or the AWS region drops, the Edges keep serving secrets from their persistent cache, even after a container restart during the outage.
flow.s10_desc: Each Edge writes audit events (authentication and secret retrieval) to audit.json and service events to edge.log in its persistence folder. A SIEM agent on the host, such as the Splunk Universal Forwarder, ships them.
flow.s11_desc: Workloads authenticate and fetch secrets from their nearby Edge or straight from Secrets Manager SaaS. A cloud workload with internet access can call the tenant directly.

secretflow.diagram_label: An application with a hardcoded, static secret
secretflow.s1_desc: A secret is anything that grants access: a database password, an API key, a token, the private key of a certificate. Here, the password of the orders database is the secret.
secretflow.s2_title: 2. The password is typed into the code
secretflow.s2_desc: To make it work quickly, the developer writes the password in a config file. This is a hardcoded, static secret, and it is the root of the problem.
secretflow.s3_title: 3. Commit: the secret is in git forever
secretflow.s3_desc: After the commit, the password lives in the repository history. Deleting the line later does not remove it: every clone and fork keeps a copy.
secretflow.s4_title: 4. Build: the secret is inside the image
secretflow.s4_desc: CI builds the container image with the config file in it. Anyone who can pull the image can read the password.
secretflow.s5_desc: The app reads the password from its own files and connects to the database. Nothing looks wrong, which is why hardcoded secrets survive for years.
secretflow.s6_title: 6. The problem: whoever has a copy gets in
secretflow.s6_desc: A clone of the repo, a pulled image, a backup or a log is enough. The database cannot tell the real app from someone using the same password.
secretflow.s7_title: 7. Rotating it means a new release
secretflow.s7_desc: To change the password you edit the code, rebuild and redeploy, and every old copy stays valid until you do. So in practice it never changes.
secretflow.s8_title: 8. The fix: no secret in the code
secretflow.s8_desc: Store the secret in a vault and let the app fetch it at runtime, proving who it is with its own identity. The next concepts show how.

idconcept.diagram_label: How a workload proves who it is with a machine identity
idconcept.n_thief_sub: an old token from a log
idconcept.s1_desc: It is how a workload (an app, a pod, a pipeline job) proves who it is, like a passport. The workload does not carry a password: its identity comes from the platform where it runs.
idconcept.s2_title: 2. The platform issues and signs it
idconcept.s2_desc: Kubernetes knows exactly which pod this is, so it hands the pod a short-lived token signed with the platform private key: namespace orders, ServiceAccount api, valid for 10 minutes.
idconcept.s3_desc: When it needs something, the workload shows that token to IDIRA. It is like showing a passport at the border: no password involved.
idconcept.s4_desc: IDIRA fetches the issuer public keys and verifies the signature. Only identities signed by a platform you trust are accepted.
idconcept.s5_title: 5. IDIRA checks the claims against policy
idconcept.s5_desc: The token says who the workload is (namespace, ServiceAccount, repository, role). IDIRA compares that with the policy to decide what this specific workload may access.
idconcept.s6_desc: IDIRA returns short-lived access (a token or the secret the policy allows), and the workload connects to the service.
idconcept.s7_title: 7. It expires and renews by itself
idconcept.s7_desc: Minutes later the token expires and the platform issues a new one automatically. Nobody rotates anything by hand.
idconcept.s8_desc: Someone finds an old token in a log and tries to use it. It has expired, and the signature, issuer and audience no longer match, so IDIRA refuses it.
idconcept.s9_desc: A machine identity is issued by the platform, verified on every request and short-lived. There is no password in the code to leak, which is what the next concepts build on.

swaarch.title: Secure Workload Access architecture
swaarch.subtitle: How IDIRA Secure Workload Access (SWA) issues SPIFFE identities to your workloads: a control plane in Secrets Manager SaaS, an SWA Server and SWA Agents in your own infrastructure.

intro.issue_desc: Workloads receive SVIDs (X.509 and JWT) after attestation. The SWA Agent renews them before they expire, with no restart.
intro.federate_desc: A JWT-SVID is exchanged for temporary AWS, Azure or Google Cloud credentials through OIDC federation.
intro.exchange_desc: Workloads that still need a password authenticate to Secrets Manager with their JWT-SVID and fetch only what policy grants.

swaarch.flow_intro: Kubernetes and VM deployments use the SWA Server and SWA Agents. The control plane, inventory, audit and public JWKS live in Secrets Manager SaaS. Ports are shown on each connection.

flow.s1_title: 1. Two halves: control plane and data plane
flow.s1_desc: SWA is a SPIFFE implementation delivered as a feature of Secrets Manager. Secrets Manager SaaS is the control plane; the SWA Server and SWA Agents run in your infrastructure and issue the identities.
flow.s2_desc: In Secrets Manager you define the trust domain, the server group and the node groups. The SWA Server, registered with an authn_id and installed with Helm, connects to the tenant over HTTPS to retrieve its configuration.
flow.s3_desc: Secrets Manager publishes the trust domain OIDC discovery document and JWKS under /.well-known. Anyone who must verify a JWT-SVID, such as a cloud provider, reads the public keys there.
flow.s4_desc: The SWA Agent runs as a DaemonSet and presents a projected service account token (k8s_psat) on TCP 8443. The SWA Server validates it against the Kubernetes API and reads the swa_nodegroup label to place the node in a node group.
flow.s5_title: 5. VMs and other clusters through a load balancer
flow.s5_desc: Agents outside the server cluster reach it through a LoadBalancer Service that forwards TCP 8443. They attest with an X.509 machine certificate (x509pop) or the AWS Instance Identity Document.
flow.s6_desc: The workload calls the Workload API on a local Unix domain socket, with no network call and no credential. The agent checks its runtime attributes (namespace, service account, labels; or uid, path and binary hash on Unix).
flow.s7_desc: The agent obtains the SVID from the server and hands the workload an X.509-SVID, a JWT-SVID and the trust bundle. SWA records the workload under data/swa/trust-domains/<trust-domain>/workloads/, with no secret access by default.
flow.s8_desc: The SPIFFE ID sits in the X.509-SVID SAN URI, so two workloads authenticate each other over mTLS without shared API keys or hand-made certificates.
flow.s9_title: 9. Cloud access with no stored keys
flow.s9_desc: payments-api requests a JWT-SVID with the cloud audience (for AWS, sts.amazonaws.com). The cloud validates it against the public JWKS of the SWA issuer and returns temporary credentials, for example through AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.
flow.s10_title: 10. Secret exchange when a credential is still needed
flow.s10_desc: For targets that are not SPIFFE-aware, orders-api presents its RSA-signed JWT-SVID to the Secrets Manager JWT authenticator, which maps the SPIFFE ID to the workload host and returns only the secrets that policy grants.
flow.s11_desc: SVIDs are short-lived and the SWA Agent renews them before they expire, with no restart. Secrets Manager keeps the workload inventory and the audit log.

swaarch.col_where: Where it runs and how it connects

sm.name: Secrets Manager SaaS (control plane)
sm.role: Defines trust domains, server groups, node groups and attestation policies. Provides the workload inventory, audit logging and the public JWKS endpoints.
sm.where: IDIRA cloud. SWA is available in US-EAST-1. Managed through the UI, REST API or the Terraform provider.

oidc.name: OIDC discovery and JWKS
oidc.role: Public issuer endpoints of each trust domain, used by relying parties and cloud providers to verify JWT-SVIDs.

server.name: SWA Server
server.role: Performs client (node) attestation, issues SVIDs and manages the trust domain signing keys. Retrieves configuration from and reports inventory to Secrets Manager.
server.where: Your Kubernetes cluster (Helm chart, namespace swa-system). Listens on 8443 for agents; replicaCount defaults to 1.

lb.name: Load balancer
lb.role: Exposes the SWA Server API to agents outside its cluster (VMs or another cluster). In-cluster agents use the Service DNS name instead.
lb.where: Kubernetes Service of type LoadBalancer forwarding TCP 8443; can be internal with cloud annotations.

agent.name: SWA Agent (Kubernetes)
agent.role: Exposes the Workload API, performs workload attestation and requests SVIDs from the server on behalf of local workloads.
agent.where: DaemonSet on every node; node attestation with k8s_psat (or k8s_jwt when the server cannot reach the API server).

vm.name: SWA Agent (VM)
vm.role: Same role on Unix or Linux machines, attesting processes with the unix workload attestor.
vm.where: System service installed with Ansible; node attestation with x509pop or AWS IID; connects to the server load balancer on 8443.

attestors.name: Node attestation
attestors.role: Verifies the connecting node before any workload on it gets an SVID: k8s_psat, k8s_jwt, x509pop or AWS IID (EC2).
attestors.where: Evaluated by the SWA Server against the server group policies; the node lands in a node group.

wapi.name: Workload API
wapi.role: Local API that workloads call to get their SVIDs and trust bundle, without network calls or pre-shared credentials.
wapi.where: Unix domain socket exposed by the agent (default /tmp/swa-agent/public/api.sock in Kubernetes).

svid.name: X.509-SVID and JWT-SVID
svid.role: Signed identity documents that prove the SPIFFE ID: X.509 for mTLS, JWT for federation and Secrets Manager authentication.
svid.where: Held by the workload; short-lived and renewed automatically by the agent.

cloud.name: Cloud federation
cloud.role: AWS IAM OIDC provider (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity), Azure federated identity credential, Google Workload Identity Federation: exchange a JWT-SVID for temporary credentials.
cloud.where: In each cloud account, trusting the public SWA issuer URL and the workload SPIFFE ID.

authn.name: Secrets Manager JWT authenticator
authn.role: Lets a workload trade its JWT-SVID for the secrets that policy grants (secret exchange).
authn.where: Secrets Manager SaaS; accepts RSA-signed JWTs only (RS* with RSA_*).

swaarch.ports_sub: Only values that the documentation gives. Where no port is documented, the protocol is shown.

p8443.path: Every SWA Agent to the SWA Server (or its load balancer)
p8443.purpose: SWA Server API: attestation and SVID requests. Must be reachable from every agent node.

pcp.path: SWA Server and agents to the tenant
pcp.purpose: Control plane configuration and the bootstrap trust bundle (.well-known/ca-bundles).

puds.path: Workload to the local SWA Agent

poidc.path: Cloud providers and verifiers to the tenant
poidc.purpose: OIDC discovery and JWKS; the issuer URL must be public and unauthenticated.

pk8s.path: SWA Server to the cluster API server
pk8s.purpose: Validates projected service account tokens for k8s_psat.

paws.purpose: ec2:DescribeInstances to verify instances attesting with AWS IID.

limits.i1: SWA is available in the US-EAST-1 region only.
limits.i2: The Secrets Manager JWT authenticator accepts RSA-signed JWTs only (RS* with RSA_*). Keep RSA signing on the trust domain for secret exchange; new trust domains default to RS512 with RSA_4096.
limits.i3: TCP 8443 on the SWA Server must be reachable from every node or VM that runs an agent; otherwise the agent fails at bootstrap and never attests.
limits.i4: For AWS and Google Cloud federation the issuer URL must be a public, unauthenticated HTTPS URL.
limits.i5: k8s_psat needs network access from the SWA Server to the Kubernetes API server; use k8s_jwt when that is not possible (for example hub and spoke).
limits.i6: New workload identities have no secret access by default: grant permissions before the workload needs secrets.
limits.i7: Migrating from another authenticator: SWA does not reuse the existing identity. Delete it, grant the new SPIFFE identity and plan a short interruption.
limits.i8: Without bootstrap.bundleSourceUrl, a server CA rotation requires a manual agent restart.
limits.i9: The agentless flow (swa_identity_sdk) applies to managed GCP compute such as Gemini Enterprise; it has no node groups and no Workload API socket.

practices.i1: Set bootstrap.bundleSourceUrl in production so agents recover automatically when the server CA rotates.
practices.i2: Expose the SWA Server through an internal load balancer when agents run outside its cluster, and open TCP 8443 early with the firewall team.
practices.i3: Restrict cloud roles to the expected SPIFFE ID (the JWT sub claim) and request the audience each provider expects.
practices.i4: Grant the SWA Server role only ec2:DescribeInstances when you use AWS IID attestation.
practices.i5: Use separate trust domains for separate administrative boundaries, such as production and non-production.
practices.i6: Prefer SPIFFE-aware access (mTLS, federation) and keep secret exchange for targets that still need a credential.
practices.i7: Manage trust domains, server groups and node groups as code with the REST API or the Terraform provider.

authnhub.title: How workloads and people prove who they are
authnhub.subtitle: IDIRA Secrets Manager never hands out a secret on trust. Every request starts with an authenticator: the caller proves its identity, receives a short-lived access token, and policy decides what that identity may read.
authnhub.what_lead: All methods end the same way. What changes is the proof the caller presents in step one.
authnhub.step_proof_desc: The caller sends its proof to the authenticate endpoint: an API key, a signed JWT, a cloud identity token, an AWS signed request or an X.509 client certificate.
authnhub.step_token_desc: If the proof is valid, Secrets Manager returns an access token signed with RSA 2048. On SaaS it lasts 8 minutes for a workload and 60 minutes for a user; then the caller authenticates again.
authnhub.step_policy_desc: Every later request carries the token. Access to each secret is granted only by permit statements in policy, so a valid identity without a grant still gets nothing.
authnhub.compare_lead: One row per method. Open a method to see the step-by-step flow and every documented limitation.
authnhub.partial_note: Partial: on SaaS, client certificates work only against a Secrets Manager Edge. On Self-Hosted, SPIFFE identities are accepted through the certificate authenticator in SPIFFE mode (X.509-SVID).

apikey.name: API key
apikey.proof: A random 51 to 56 character API key generated by Secrets Manager
apikey.stored: Yes: the API key (file or environment variables)
apikey.limit: It is a secret zero: anyone with a copy authenticates until the key is rotated

jwt.name: JWT
jwt.proof: A JWT signed by a trusted provider, checked against its JWKS and claims
jwt.limit: On Self-Hosted, claims that contain a forward slash (/) are not supported

iam.name: AWS IAM
iam.who: AWS resources that support IAM roles
iam.proof: A signed STS GetCallerIdentity request built from the IAM role session
iam.limit: On SaaS it is documented as a legacy cloud authenticator: new cloud workloads should use SWA

azure.name: Azure
azure.who: Azure VMs, App Services, Functions and Container Instances
azure.proof: An Azure-issued token for the resource identity
azure.limit: Only the documented Azure services are supported

gcp.name: Google Cloud
gcp.proof: A Google-signed identity token from the metadata server
gcp.limit: Only one GCP authenticator can exist (conjur/authn-gcp)

cert.name: Client certificate
cert.who: Workloads such as VMs and IoT devices
cert.proof: An X.509 client certificate presented over mutual TLS
cert.limit: On SaaS it works only with a Secrets Manager Edge

k8s.name: Kubernetes (certificate)
k8s.proof: A certificate-based mutual TLS flow for Kubernetes resources
k8s.limit: Self-Hosted only; on SaaS, Kubernetes uses the JWT authenticator

spiffe.name: SPIFFE / SWA
spiffe.proof: A short-lived X.509-SVID or JWT-SVID issued by Secure Workload Access
spiffe.limit: Requires the SWA server and agents; JWT-SVIDs are validated by a JWT authenticator

users.name: People
users.proof: SaaS: sign-in through Identity (SSO and MFA). Self-Hosted: password or API key, LDAP or OIDC
users.limit: LDAP is a Self-Hosted authenticator; SaaS users are managed in Identity

authnhub.limits_title: Rules that apply to every authenticator
limits: Authenticator service IDs cannot be nested: conjur/authn-azure/sysadmins is valid, conjur/authn-azure/sysadmins/new is not.
Access tokens are short-lived (8 minutes for workloads on SaaS and Self-Hosted); the caller must authenticate again when the token expires.
A valid identity is not enough: the workload also needs authenticate permission on the authenticator and permit grants on each secret.
Self-Hosted: every authenticator except the default one must be allowlisted (conjur.yml or CONJUR_AUTHENTICATORS); when CONJUR_AUTHENTICATORS is set, only the listed authenticators are allowed.
Self-Hosted: values set with evoke variable set do not persist across upgrades and are lost when a Standby is promoted to Leader; use conjur.yml or environment variables.
SaaS: creating, updating and deleting authenticators requires membership in Authn_Admins (or Conjur_Cloud_Admins).
SaaS: the AWS IAM, Azure and GCP authenticators are documented as legacy paths; for new cloud workloads the documentation recommends Secure Workload Access.

authn_apikey.title: API key authentication (authn)
authn_apikey.subtitle: The default authenticator: the workload proves who it is with a random API key generated by Secrets Manager. It is simple and works everywhere, but the key is a stored secret, so it must be protected and rotated.
authn_apikey.roles_lead: Who holds what in an API key authentication.
roles: Host (workload)
The identity in policy. Its login is host/ plus the full policy path, URL-encoded in requests (host%2Fdata%2Fapp).
API key
Random 51 to 56 character string generated by Secrets Manager when the host is created; the password equivalent of the host.
Credential storage
A file such as /etc/conjur.identity, or the environment variables CONJUR_AUTHN_LOGIN and CONJUR_AUTHN_API_KEY.
authn endpoint
POST /authn/{account}/{login}/authenticate (SaaS: /api/authn/conjur/{login}/authenticate). The body is the API key.
Access token
JWT signed with RSA 2048, 8 minutes for a workload. Sent as Authorization: Token token="..." on every request.
Policy
permit statements decide which secrets the host may read; without them the token gives no access.
when: Legacy servers, VMs or scripts that cannot use an identity-based authenticator.
Quick tests and proofs of concept.
Workloads behind a Secrets Manager Edge, which supports local API key authentication.
Short-lived workloads only through Host Factory or an integration that manages the identity.
limits: The API key is a secret zero: it must be stored with the workload (file or environment variables) and protected like any password.
Anyone who obtains a copy of the key can authenticate as that host until the key is rotated.
The key is always a random value generated by Secrets Manager; it cannot be set to a value you choose.
Rotation is a manual action (UI, CLI or API): the new key must be replaced everywhere the old one was used, and the UI shows the new key only once.
Users with the appropriate permission on the host can read its current API key: limit who has that permission.
The access token expires after 8 minutes (workload); the client must authenticate again to keep working.
The login must be URL-encoded in the request path (slashes become %2F).
For new cloud workloads the SaaS documentation recommends Secure Workload Access instead of stored credentials.
diff: Endpoint
SaaS: https://<subdomain>.secretsmgr.cyberark.cloud/api/authn/conjur/{login}/authenticate (or the Edge host). Self-Hosted: https://<server>/authn/{account}/{login}/authenticate.
Users
SaaS: people sign in through Identity. Self-Hosted: users also get an API key and can set a password (stored with bcrypt) after the first login.
Configuration
Both: no configuration needed for authn. Self-Hosted: if CONJUR_AUTHENTICATORS is set, authn must be in the list.
Token lifetime
Both: 8 minutes for a workload. SaaS documents 60 minutes for a user identity.

flow.diagram_label: API key authentication to IDIRA Secrets Manager, step by step
flow.s1_desc: API key authentication (authn) is built in and needs no configuration. The workload is a host in policy; its login is host/ followed by its full policy path, for example host/data/app.
flow.s2_desc: When the host is created (policy load or the UI), Secrets Manager generates a random API key of 51 to 56 characters and returns it in the output. Nobody chooses the value.
flow.s3_title: 3. The key is stored with the workload
flow.s3_desc: Long-running workloads keep it in a file such as /etc/conjur.identity; containers and CI jobs receive CONJUR_AUTHN_LOGIN and CONJUR_AUTHN_API_KEY as environment variables. This stored key is the secret zero.
flow.s4_desc: At startup the application, SDK or CLI reads the login and the API key from the file or the environment.
flow.s5_desc: The workload sends POST /authn/{account}/{login}/authenticate with the API key as the body and the URL-encoded login (host%2Fdata%2Fapp). On SaaS the path is /api/authn/conjur/... on your tenant or Edge.
flow.s6_desc: If the key matches, Secrets Manager returns an access token: a JWT signed with RSA 2048, valid for 8 minutes for a workload. With Accept-Encoding: base64 it comes ready to use in a header.
flow.s7_title: 7. Policy decides, the secret is returned
flow.s7_desc: The workload calls the secrets API with Authorization: Token token="...". Secrets Manager returns the secret only if policy grants read and execute on it to this host.
flow.s8_desc: When it expires, requests are rejected and the workload authenticates again with the same API key. SDKs and the CLI do this automatically.
flow.s9_title: 9. The risk: a copied key works
flow.s9_desc: Anyone who obtains the file, the environment variable or a log containing the key can authenticate as this host. Users with the right permission can also read the current key.
flow.s10_desc: An admin rotates the key in the UI, CLI or API. The UI shows the new key only once; it must be replaced everywhere the old one was used, and from then on the old copies are rejected.

authn_cert.title: Client certificate authentication (authn-cert)
authn_cert.subtitle: The workload proves who it is with an X.509 client certificate over mutual TLS, checked against your CA bundle, an optional revocation list and the workload annotations. Nothing reusable travels on the wire.
authn_cert.support_note: On SaaS, certificate authentication works only against a Secrets Manager Edge.
authn_cert.roles_lead: What each part does in a certificate authentication.
roles: Certificate authority
Issues the client certificate. Its root (and any intermediates) is the trust anchor configured in the authenticator.
Certificate authenticator
Policy under conjur/authn-cert/<name> with the ca-cert variable (PEM bundle) and optionally crl or crl-url; it must be enabled.
Groups apps and operators
Members of apps can authenticate with the authenticator; members of operators can update it.
Workload (host)
Holds the client certificate and its private key, has at least one certificate annotation and belongs to the apps group.
Secrets Manager or Edge
Terminates the mTLS handshake, validates chain, CRL/CDP and annotations, and issues the access token. On SaaS this is the Edge.
Policy
Consumer groups on each secret decide what the authenticated workload can fetch.
authn_cert.annot_lead: Define at least one. Each certificate field you list must match the client certificate.
annotations: A comma-delimited list of URIs, for example spiffe://acme.dev/workloads/vm-01
A comma-delimited list of DNS names
A comma-delimited list of IP addresses
when: VMs and IoT devices that already receive certificates from a corporate CA.
Environments where a workload certificate is the natural identity and no JWT or cloud identity is available.
Workloads served by a nearby Secrets Manager Edge (SaaS).
Self-Hosted workloads with X.509-SVIDs, using the SPIFFE host mode.
limits: SaaS: client certificate authentication is only available for authenticating workloads to a Secrets Manager Edge, not to the SaaS tenant directly.
The CA bundle must be PEM and contain exactly one root CA (intermediates are allowed); the client certificate chain must resolve to that root.
The workload must have at least one annotation (san-uri, san-dns, san-ip or cn), and at least one annotation must be validated for the request to succeed.
You cannot define both crl and crl-url; CRL URLs must use http or https (any other scheme, including LDAP, makes CRL retrieval and authentication fail).
If the client certificate contains a cRLDistributionPoints field, it is always validated against that CDP.
The workload keeps the certificate private key: protect it and plan certificate renewal with your CA.
Creating the authenticator and granting workload permissions on it require Authn_Admins membership (SaaS) or create privileges on the conjur/authn-cert policy.
The authenticator must be enabled before workloads can use it.
SaaS UI: the data/ branch for the workload must already exist; creating it requires the CLI.
diff: Where to authenticate

SaaS: only a Secrets Manager Edge, at https://<edge>/api/authn-cert/{name}/conjur/{host}/authenticate. Self-Hosted: Secrets Manager itself, at https://<server>/authn-cert/{name}/{account}[/{host}]/authenticate.
Host mapping
Self-Hosted adds host-mode: request (default, host in the path, annotations required) or spiffe (host derived from the X.509-SVID SPIFFE ID using trust-domain and identity-path).
Authenticator restrictions
Self-Hosted can also restrict the authenticator itself with san-uri, san-dns, san-ip and cn variables (with documented wildcard rules).
Configuration
SaaS: UI or policy, then conjur authenticator enable. Self-Hosted: policy, and the authenticator must be allowlisted like any non-default authenticator.

authn_cert.doc_sh_api: Authenticate with a client certificate (Self-Hosted API)

flow.diagram_label: Client certificate authentication to IDIRA Secrets Manager, step by step
flow.s1_desc: With authn-cert the workload proves who it is with an X.509 client certificate over mutual TLS (TLS 1.3 by default, or 1.2). No password is sent; the workload keeps the certificate private key.
flow.s2_desc: Under conjur/authn-cert, a policy defines the authenticator (for example acme-vm) with the ca-cert variable: a PEM bundle with exactly one root CA and any intermediates. A CRL (crl) or CRL URL (crl-url) is optional; then the authenticator is enabled.
flow.s3_title: 3. The workload is defined with annotations
flow.s3_desc: The workload (host) joins the authenticator apps group and gets at least one annotation (san-uri, san-dns, san-ip or cn). Those certificate fields must match for the request to succeed.
flow.s4_title: 4. The CA issues the client certificate
flow.s4_desc: Your certificate authority issues the client certificate and key. Its chain of trust must resolve to the root CA in the authenticator bundle.
flow.s5_desc: The workload sends POST /authn-cert/{name}/{account}/{host}/authenticate with its certificate and key. The TLS handshake happens before the HTTP request. On SaaS the target is a Secrets Manager Edge (/api/authn-cert/...).
flow.s6_desc: If a CRL is defined, the certificate is checked against it. If the certificate has a cRLDistributionPoints field, it is always checked against that CDP too. CRL URLs must use http or https.
flow.s7_desc: The certificate fields are compared with the workload annotations. An annotation scoped to the authenticator (authn-cert/acme-vm/san-uri) takes precedence over a global one (authn-cert/san-uri).
flow.s8_desc: If everything matches, the workload receives an access token (8 minutes for a workload), exactly like the other authenticators.
flow.s9_desc: With the token the workload fetches its secrets. It needs to be in the consumer group of each secret; policy decides.
flow.s10_desc: SaaS: certificate authentication only works against a Secrets Manager Edge. Self-Hosted: the workload authenticates directly, and a SPIFFE mode can derive the host from an X.509-SVID.

authn_aws.flow_title: How it works today, step by step
authn_aws.title: AWS IAM authenticator
authn_aws.subtitle: An AWS workload proves who it is with the IAM role it already runs with. It signs an AWS STS GetCallerIdentity request and IDIRA Secrets Manager asks STS who signed it. No API key or password is stored on the workload.
authn_aws.flow_lead: The workload never sends its AWS keys: it sends a signed request that only STS can validate, and Secrets Manager compares the answer with the workload ID.
authn_aws.how_lead: What each piece does and how the workload identity is written.
roles: AWS workload
Any AWS resource that supports IAM roles (EC2, ECS, Lambda). It runs with an IAM role and signs the STS request with that role's session credentials (SigV4).
IAM role credentials
Temporary session credentials of the role, from the instance metadata service (169.254.169.254) or the Lambda environment.
authn-iam/{service-id}
The AWS IAM authenticator in Secrets Manager. SaaS ships a predefined authn-iam/default; you can create more under conjur/authn-iam.
Workload ID (host)
Must match the AWS account ID and role name: AccountID/RoleName, for example 111111111111/IAMConjurRole (under your branch, such as data/myspace).
apps group
Hosts that belong to conjur/authn-iam/{service-id}/apps may authenticate with this authenticator.
AWS STS
Secrets Manager replays the signed GetCallerIdentity request; STS returns the caller Arn and Account, which must match the host.
Access token
Short-lived Secrets Manager token (8 minutes) used to read the secrets the policy allows.
when: Workloads on EC2, ECS, Lambda or any AWS service that runs with an IAM role.
You want to remove the API key (secret zero) from AWS workloads.
One identity per IAM role is the right granularity for your applications.
diff: SaaS: enable the predefined authn-iam/default authenticator (UI, APIv2 or CLI) or create one under conjur/authn-iam. Self-Hosted: define the conjur/authn-iam/{service-id} policy and allowlist authn-iam/{service-id}.
Endpoint. SaaS: POST /api/authn-iam/{service-id}/conjur/{host-id}/authenticate. Self-Hosted: POST /authn-iam/{service-id}/{account}/{host-id}/authenticate.
Self-Hosted documents the optional-signed-headers variable to accept extra signed headers; by default only host and x-amz-* headers are allowed.
Validity of the signed request: the Self-Hosted docs say five minutes; the SaaS docs describe the signed session credentials as typically valid for 15 minutes.
limits: The workload ID must be exactly AccountID/RoleName of the AWS resource; a different Arn returns 401.
The workload must be a member of the authenticator apps group; granting it requires update permission on the authenticator (Authn_Admins or Conjur_Cloud_Admins in SaaS).
SaaS docs: add the documented STS permission (sts:* on the role Arn) to the IAM role.
The signing region must match the STS endpoint sent to Secrets Manager; with the global endpoint sts.amazonaws.com the request must be signed with us-east-1.
STS endpoints in China (.cn) are not supported (Self-Hosted docs).
Signed requests expire: a request signed by an unknown key or older than its validity window is rejected with 401.
Only the required signed headers (host and x-amz-*) are accepted unless optional-signed-headers is set (Self-Hosted).
Your code must build the SigV4 signed GetCallerIdentity request (Python, Ruby or Bash examples; a Python client exists).
The access token lasts 8 minutes; the workload must authenticate again after that.
docs: Set up AWS resources and usage (SaaS)

flow.diagram_label: AWS IAM authentication to IDIRA Secrets Manager
flow.s1_title: 1. The workload runs with an IAM role
flow.s1_desc: The AWS resource (EC2, ECS, Lambda) was started with an IAM role. In Secrets Manager it is represented by a workload ID named after that role: AccountID/RoleName.
flow.s2_title: 2. It gets the role session credentials
flow.s2_desc: AWS hands the workload temporary credentials for its role, from the instance metadata service or the Lambda environment. They never leave the workload.
flow.s3_desc: The workload builds an STS GetCallerIdentity request and signs it with SigV4. Only the signed headers (Host, X-Amz-Date, X-Amz-Security-Token, Authorization) will be sent.
flow.s4_desc: The signed headers go in the body of POST /authn-iam/{service-id}/conjur/{host-id}/authenticate. Secrets Manager first checks that the host belongs to the authenticator apps group.
flow.s5_title: 5. Secrets Manager asks STS who signed it
flow.s5_desc: Secrets Manager replays the signed request to AWS STS. STS answers with the caller Arn and account, and Secrets Manager checks that they match the host AccountID/RoleName.
flow.s6_title: 6. It returns a short-lived access token
flow.s6_desc: When the roles match, Secrets Manager returns an access token valid for 8 minutes.
flow.s7_desc: With the token, the workload requests the secrets its policy allows (for example a Safe consumers group) and keeps them in memory.
flow.s8_desc: The workload uses the credential to reach the database or API. Nothing was stored in code, image or configuration.

authn_azure.flow_title: How it works today, step by step
authn_azure.title: Azure authenticator
authn_azure.subtitle: An Azure workload proves who it is with an Azure AD token from the Instance Metadata Service. IDIRA Secrets Manager checks the token issuer and matches the subscription, resource group and, optionally, the managed identity on the workload ID. No secret zero to store.
authn_azure.flow_lead: The workload asks Azure for a signed token and hands it to Secrets Manager, which decides based on Azure attributes written as host annotations.
authn_azure.how_lead: What each piece does and which annotations identify the Azure resource.
roles: Azure workload
A workload on Azure Virtual Machines, App Services, Functions or Container Instances.
Azure IMDS
The Instance Metadata Service (169.254.169.254) returns a signed Azure AD token (JWT) for the resource, optionally for a specific managed identity.
authn-azure/{service-id}
The Azure authenticator, always under conjur/authn-azure. Its provider-uri variable holds the Azure provider: https://sts.windows.net/{tenant_id}/.
Workload ID (host)
Must carry authn-azure/subscription-id and authn-azure/resource-group annotations; optionally authn-azure/user-assigned-identity or authn-azure/system-assigned-identity (one of them).
apps group
Hosts in the authenticator apps group may authenticate with it.
Access token
Short-lived Secrets Manager token (8 minutes) used to read the secrets the policy allows.
when: Workloads on Azure VMs, App Services, Functions or Container Instances.
You want one identity for a whole resource group, or one per resource using managed identities.
You want to replace API key authentication on Azure (no secret zero).
diff: Endpoint. SaaS: POST /api/authn-azure/{service-id}/conjur/{host-id}/authenticate. Self-Hosted: POST /authn-azure/{service-id}/{account}/{host-id}/authenticate.

SaaS: create the authenticator in the UI or by policy under conjur/authn-azure (Authn_Admins or Conjur_Cloud_Admins), set provider-uri and enable it. Self-Hosted: load the policy, set provider-uri and allowlist authn-azure/{service-id}.
The identification model (subscription, resource group, optional managed identity) is the same in both.
limits: Supported Azure services: Virtual Machines, App Services, Functions and Container Instances only.
Every host must have the subscription ID and resource group annotations (case-sensitive in the Self-Hosted docs).
Managed identity is optional, but use either the system-assigned or the user-assigned identity, never both.
A system-assigned identity only exists after the resource is created, so its host policy must be loaded at run time by your pipeline; user-assigned identities can be declared in advance.
The provider-uri variable (https://sts.windows.net/{tenant_id}/) must be set and the authenticator enabled before workloads can authenticate.
Request the token from IMDS with api-version 2018-02-01 or later; with a system-assigned identity it must be enabled in Azure first.
The host ID in the URL must be the full host name, URL encoded (for example host%2Fdata%2Fazure-apps%2FazureVM).
Granting the host permission to authenticate requires update permission on the authenticator (SaaS: Authn_Admins or Conjur_Cloud_Admins).
The access token lasts 8 minutes; the workload must authenticate again after that.
docs: Authenticate using the Azure authenticator API (SaaS)

flow.diagram_label: Azure authentication to IDIRA Secrets Manager
flow.s1_desc: The Azure resource is represented in Secrets Manager by a workload ID annotated with its subscription and resource group, and optionally one managed identity.
flow.s2_title: 2. It asks IMDS for an Azure AD token
flow.s2_desc: The workload calls the Instance Metadata Service at 169.254.169.254 (/metadata/identity/oauth2/token, api-version 2018-02-01 or later) and receives a signed JWT.
flow.s3_title: 3. It sends the token to authn-azure
flow.s3_desc: POST /authn-azure/{service-id}/conjur/{host-id}/authenticate with jwt=... in the body and the host ID URL encoded. Secrets Manager checks that the host belongs to the authenticator apps group.
flow.s4_desc: The token must be valid and issued by the provider configured in the authenticator (provider-uri, https://sts.windows.net/{tenant_id}/).
flow.s5_desc: The subscription, resource group and, if annotated, the user-assigned or system-assigned identity in the token must match the host annotations.
flow.s6_title: 6. It returns a short-lived access token
flow.s6_desc: If everything matches, Secrets Manager returns an access token valid for 8 minutes.
flow.s7_desc: With the token, the workload requests the secrets its policy allows and keeps them in memory.
flow.s8_desc: The workload uses the credential to reach the database or API, with no secret zero stored anywhere.

authn_gcp.flow_title: How it works today, step by step
authn_gcp.title: GCP authenticator
authn_gcp.subtitle: A Google Cloud workload proves who it is with a Google-signed identity token from the metadata server. The token audience is its Secrets Manager workload ID, and IDIRA Secrets Manager matches the token claims against the workload annotations.
authn_gcp.flow_lead: The workload never holds a key: Google issues an identity token for its service account, scoped by audience to one Secrets Manager host.
authn_gcp.how_lead: What each piece does and how claims map to annotations.
roles: GCP workload
A workload on Google Compute Engine or Google Cloud Functions, running with a service account.
Google metadata server
Returns a Google-signed identity token (JWT) for the service account, with the requested audience. For GCE it must be requested in full format.
authn-gcp
The GCP authenticator, always in the conjur/authn-gcp policy branch. Only one can exist.
Workload ID (host)

Annotated with authn-gcp/instance-name (GCE), authn-gcp/project-id (GCE), authn-gcp/service-account-id (sub claim) and/or authn-gcp/service-account-email (email claim). All annotations must match (AND).
Audience
The token aud claim is the full Secrets Manager host ID, for example conjur/conjur/host/data/myspace/gcp-apps/test-app. Secrets Manager resolves the host from it.
Access token
Short-lived Secrets Manager token (8 minutes) used to read the secrets the policy allows.
when: Workloads on Google Compute Engine or Google Cloud Functions.
You want identity based on the GCP service account (and, on GCE, the instance and project) with no stored secret.
You can request an identity token with a custom audience from your code.
diff: Endpoint. SaaS: POST /api/authn-gcp/conjur/authenticate. Self-Hosted: POST /authn-gcp/{account}/authenticate. Neither carries the host ID in the URL.
SaaS: enable the predefined GCP authenticator (UI, APIv2 or CLI); create one only if it does not exist. Self-Hosted: load the conjur/authn-gcp policy and allowlist authn-gcp.
Audience format. SaaS example: conjur/conjur/host/data/myspace/... . Self-Hosted example: conjur/{account}/host/... .
limits: Supported Google Cloud services: Compute Engine and Cloud Functions only.
Only one GCP authenticator can be configured.
The identity token audience must be the full Secrets Manager host ID; a token for another audience is rejected.
On GCE the token must be requested in full format (format=full) so it carries the instance and project claims.
Use at least one annotation; authn-gcp/instance-name must be combined with another one, and instance-name and project-id work on GCE only.
Annotations are combined with AND: every annotated value must match its claim.
Do not put the host ID in the authenticate URL: the host comes from the token, and adding it causes a 401 error.
Google recommends a user-managed service account on Compute Engine instead of the default service account.
The access token lasts 8 minutes; the workload must authenticate again after that.
docs: Authenticate using the GCP authenticator API (SaaS)

flow.diagram_label: GCP authentication to IDIRA Secrets Manager
flow.s1_title: 1. The workload runs on Google Cloud
flow.s1_desc: The GCE instance or Cloud Function runs with a service account. In Secrets Manager it is a workload ID annotated with authn-gcp/* values.
flow.s2_title: 2. It asks the metadata server for an identity token
flow.s2_desc: The workload requests an identity token with audience set to its full host ID (and format=full on GCE). The metadata server returns a Google-signed JWT with claims about the service and its identity.
flow.s3_title: 3. It sends the token to authn-gcp
flow.s3_desc: POST /authn-gcp/conjur/authenticate with jwt=... in the body. The URL has no host ID.
flow.s4_title: 4. Secrets Manager finds the host from the audience
flow.s4_desc: Secrets Manager verifies the Google token and reads its aud claim to know which workload ID is asking.
flow.s5_desc: instance-name, project-id, service-account-id (sub) and service-account-email (email) must all match the claims (AND), and the host must be in the authenticator apps group.
flow.s6_title: 6. It returns a short-lived access token
flow.s6_desc: If everything matches, Secrets Manager returns an access token valid for 8 minutes.
flow.s7_desc: With the token, the workload requests the secrets its policy allows and keeps them in memory.
flow.s8_desc: The workload uses the credential to reach the database or API, with no key stored in the instance or the function.

authn_k8s.title: Kubernetes authenticator (authn-k8s)
authn_k8s.subtitle: The native, certificate-based way for pods to prove who they are to IDIRA Secrets Manager Self-Hosted: the authenticator client asks for a certificate, a Follower inside the cluster verifies the pod with the Kubernetes API and injects the certificate, and the pod then authenticates over mutual TLS.

flow.n_api_sub: verifies the pod, injects the cert
flow.s1_desc: The Kubernetes Authenticator Client runs in the same pod as your application, as a sidecar or init container. It talks to the Kubernetes authenticator on a Secrets Manager Follower that runs inside the cluster.
flow.s2_desc: The Secrets Manager admin loads the authn-k8s/<service-id> policy, creates a CA whose key and certificate are stored in Secrets Manager variables, and allowlists the authenticator. The Kubernetes admin prepares the cluster: namespace, service account, cluster role and the Golden ConfigMap.
flow.s3_desc: The client sends a Certificate Signing Request. Its metadata carries the host identity the pod wants to use and information about the pod making the request.
flow.s4_title: 4. Secrets Manager checks the pod in Kubernetes
flow.s4_desc: The Follower asks the Kubernetes API whether that pod is legitimate and whether it may authenticate as the requested host identity (namespace, Deployment, StatefulSet and so on).
flow.s5_title: 5. The certificate is injected into the pod
flow.s5_desc: If the checks pass, the client certificate is injected into the application pod through the Kubernetes API. It is delivered out of band, not in the HTTP response, so only the pod that matches the CSR receives it.
flow.s6_title: 6. Mutual TLS and a short-lived token
flow.s6_desc: With its certificate the client opens a mutual TLS connection and requests a short-lived access token. The token is written to a volume shared with the application container.
flow.s7_desc: The application uses the access token with one of the retrieval methods (API, Summon, Secrets Provider or Secretless) and connects to its target service.
flow.s8_desc: The certificate expires and is renewed automatically on a regular basis, which limits how long a compromised certificate could be used.
flow.s9_desc: authn-k8s calls the Kubernetes API several times per authentication; authn-jwt needs one JWKS call or none. The SaaS edition documents only the JWT-based Kubernetes integration.

authn_k8s.how_lead: Each component and its role in certificate-based authentication.
authn_k8s.role_client_b: Runs in the application pod (sidecar or init container), sends the CSR, opens mutual TLS and writes the access token to the shared volume.
authn_k8s.role_follower_b: Read-only replica of the Leader running in its own namespace; hosts the Kubernetes authenticator and serves authentication and secret reads.
authn_k8s.role_api_b: Secrets Manager calls it to verify the pod and to inject the client certificate. Secrets Manager stores its URL, CA certificate and a service account token.
authn_k8s.role_ca_b: Private key and root certificate generated by the admin and kept in the conjur/authn-k8s/<service-id>/ca/key and ca/cert variables; it signs the client certificates.
authn_k8s.role_host_b: A host in policy annotated with the Kubernetes attributes allowed to use it (see the table below).
authn_k8s.role_volume_b: Memory volume in the pod where the client writes the access token for the application.
authn_k8s.ids_title: Which Kubernetes resource is the identity
authn_k8s.ids_lead: The host is matched by annotations. Pick the narrowest scope that fits how your workloads share secrets.
authn_k8s.id_namespace_b: Everything in the namespace shares the same grants.
authn_k8s.id_labels_b: Namespaces matching a label selector (for example a Rancher project).
authn_k8s.id_deployment_b: A Deployment name within a namespace.
authn_k8s.id_deploymentconfig_b: An OpenShift DeploymentConfig name within a project.
authn_k8s.id_statefulset_b: A StatefulSet name within a namespace.
authn_k8s.id_serviceaccount_b: A service account within a namespace. Recommended only as a transition towards Deployment or StatefulSet.
authn_k8s.id_pod_b: Names the container that authenticates; Pod-level identity is meant for testing and proofs of concept only.
authn_k8s.cmp_lead: Both authenticate Kubernetes workloads. The site covers authn-jwt in detail on the JWT authentication page.
authn_k8s.cmp_editions_k8s: Self-Hosted. The SaaS documentation describes the Kubernetes integration with the JWT authenticator.
authn_k8s.cmp_identity_k8s: Namespace, label selector, Deployment, DeploymentConfig, StatefulSet, service account or Pod.
authn_k8s.cmp_identity_jwt: Claims of the service account token, mainly namespace and service account.
authn_k8s.cmp_performance_k8s: Several calls to the Kubernetes API for each authentication.
authn_k8s.cmp_performance_jwt: One call to the JWKS endpoint, or none depending on configuration; usually faster.
authn_k8s.cmp_setup_k8s: Needs a cluster role, a service account token stored in Secrets Manager and a CA per service ID.
authn_k8s.cmp_setup_jwt: More straightforward in high-scale deployments and needs fewer special privileges.
authn_k8s.cmp_maintenance_k8s: Certificates and the CA must be managed, rotated and stored securely.
authn_k8s.cmp_maintenance_jwt: Service account tokens are signed; their signing keys need management.
authn_k8s.cmp_network_k8s: Secrets Manager must reach the Kubernetes API server.
authn_k8s.cmp_network_jwt: Secrets Manager reads the JWKS endpoint or uses configured public keys.
when: You run IDIRA Secrets Manager Self-Hosted with Followers inside the cluster.
You need identities finer than namespace and service account, such as a Deployment or StatefulSet.
You want mutual TLS between the workload and Secrets Manager.
limits: Self-Hosted only: the SaaS Kubernetes integration uses the JWT authenticator (authn-jwt).
The Kubernetes client in Secrets Manager must reach the Kubernetes API server. With a proxy in between, set https_proxy and http_proxy on each node.
Setup needs both a Secrets Manager admin and a Kubernetes cluster admin, plus Secrets Manager CLI v9 or later.

Secrets Manager keeps a service account token, the API URL and the cluster CA certificate in conjur/authn-k8s/<service-id>/kubernetes variables, and the cluster role grants RBAC permissions to that service account.
Kubernetes v1.24 and later do not create service account secrets automatically: use the cluster preparation Helm chart v0.2.1 or later, or create the secret by hand.
Each service ID needs its own CA (ca/key and ca/cert variables) and must be allowlisted on the nodes, for example authn-k8s/dev-cluster.
The authenticator client must run in the same pod as the application, as a sidecar or init container.
Pod-level identity is for testing only, and service-account identity is recommended only as a transition.
Each authentication makes several Kubernetes API calls, so performance is usually lower than with authn-jwt.

authn_users.title: How people sign in
authn_users.subtitle: Administrators and developers authenticate to IDIRA Secrets Manager differently from workloads. In SaaS every user comes from Identity; in Self-Hosted you can use OIDC, LDAP or the built-in user name with password or API key.
authn_users.people_note: This page is about people (UI, CLI and admin API calls). Workloads such as apps, pods and pipelines should use a workload authenticator: JWT, Kubernetes, AWS, Azure, GCP, certificate or API key.

flow.diagram_label: How human users authenticate to Secrets Manager SaaS and Self-Hosted
flow.s1_desc: Users sign in to the UI and CLI and call admin APIs. How they do it depends on the edition: SaaS on top, Self-Hosted below.
flow.s2_desc: Every Secrets Manager SaaS user is a user of the Identity Security Platform (ISPSS). The CLI login or the UI prompts for user name and password and, if configured, a multi-factor challenge. Federated users are sent to their external IdP in the browser.
flow.s3_title: 3. SaaS: ID token to Secrets Manager
flow.s3_desc: The ID token from Identity is posted to the authn-oidc/cyberark/conjur/authenticate endpoint, which returns a Secrets Manager access token. A user token lasts 60 minutes; a workload token lasts 8.
flow.s4_title: 4. SaaS: users and roles sync from Identity
flow.s4_desc: Users, groups and roles that have a Secrets Manager role in Identity (for example Conjur_Cloud_Admins or Conjur_Cloud_Users) sync to Secrets Manager. Changes show up on the next sync cycle.
flow.s5_title: 5. Self-Hosted: OIDC for UI and CLI
flow.s5_desc: The authn-oidc authenticator redirects the user to the organization IdP using the authorization code flow with PKCE. The UI or CLI hands the code to Secrets Manager, which completes the exchange with the IdP and returns an access token (1 hour by default, 5 hours at most).
flow.s6_desc: With authn-ldap the user signs in with corporate credentials and Secrets Manager performs an LDAP bind against the directory. The directory authenticates; Secrets Manager policy still decides what the user may access.
flow.s7_title: 7. Self-Hosted: user name and API key
flow.s7_desc: The default authenticator (authn) logs in with user name and password or API key at /authn/{account}/login and returns an API key; the CLI caches it and exchanges it for 8 minute access tokens.
flow.s8_desc: SaaS centralizes people in Identity with SSO and MFA. Self-Hosted lets you choose OIDC, LDAP or built-in credentials. In both, policy grants decide what each user can do.

authn_users.how_lead: Which method exists in each edition, how it works and how long the resulting token lasts.
authn_users.m_saas_how: UI or CLI login with user name, password and MFA, or an external IdP in the browser; the Identity ID token is sent to authn-oidc/cyberark/conjur.
authn_users.m_oidc_how: Authorization code flow with PKCE against your IdP, for the UI and the CLI.
authn_users.m_oidc_token: 1 hour by default, configurable up to 5 hours (token-ttl).
authn_users.m_ldap_how: LDAP bind with corporate credentials; optional just-in-time provisioning creates users from LDAP groups.
authn_users.m_ldap_token: Signed bearer token or API key, like the default authenticator.
authn_users.m_apikey_how: Login with password or API key at /authn/{account}/login; the CLI caches the API key.
authn_users.role_identity_b: SaaS identity provider: users, SSO, MFA and roles that grant Secrets Manager access.
authn_users.role_idp_b: Your IdP for Self-Hosted UI and CLI sign-in. Tested with Idira Identity, Okta and Keycloak.
authn_users.role_ldap_b: Corporate directory that authenticates users with a bind; Secrets Manager keeps authorization.
authn_users.role_cli_b: Runs the login and caches credentials: OS credential store in SaaS, .netrc (or a netrc_path) in Self-Hosted.
authn_users.role_policy_b: Users must exist in policy (or be synced or provisioned) and only get what permit statements grant.
limits_saas: Every user needs an Identity user with a Secrets Manager role; changes reach Secrets Manager on the next sync cycle.
Nested groups sync up to 10 levels deep; deeper users are added as members of the tenth level.
You cannot add several Identity entities with the same name to the built-in roles Conjur_Cloud_Admins and Conjur_Cloud_Users.
Renaming a user, group or role in Identity means reassigning its permissions in Secrets Manager.
A password passed with conjur login -p stays in the shell history; clean it at the end of the session.
The CLI stores the user name and access token in the OS credential store, or in the conjur_credentials file if there is none.
limits_sh: OIDC is for UI and CLI sign-in only: the POST authn-oidc endpoint for workloads is no longer supported; workloads use authn-jwt.
The UI and the CLI need separate OIDC authenticators.
OIDC was tested only with Idira Identity, Okta and Keycloak.
The CLI must be able to open a browser: OIDC does not work from Docker or other headless environments.
The Secrets Manager server and the user client must reach the IdP on port 443.
Only users defined in the root policy can authenticate with OIDC, and users added or removed in the IdP must be added or removed in Secrets Manager.
Do not share one OIDC issuer across tenants; keep the Secrets Manager and IdP clocks aligned.
When LDAP authentication is enabled on a node, every UI user on that node must use LDAP credentials; built-in passwords and API keys stop working for the UI.
Each LDAP user needs a user declared in policy, unless just-in-time provisioning is enabled (CLI 9.3 or later).
LDAP changes are not picked up automatically; disabled directory accounts need an extra step to lose access.
The CLI caches credentials in .netrc by default; point netrc_path to /dev/shm for a more secure setup.
